name: New York

events.title: Ratified the Constitution
events.text: New York ratified the Constitution on July 26, 1788, the 11th state to do so. The Constitution gave it 6 seats in the House until the first census.

events.title: 1790 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1790 census, New York's House delegation grew from 6 to 10 seats.

events.title: 1800 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1800 census, New York's House delegation grew from 10 to 17 seats.

events.title: 1810 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1810 census, New York's House delegation grew from 17 to 27 seats.

events.title: 1820 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1820 census, New York's House delegation grew from 27 to 34 seats.

events.title: 1830 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1830 census, New York's House delegation grew from 34 to 40 seats.

events.title: 1840 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1840 census, New York's House delegation shrank from 40 to 34 seats.

events.title: 1850 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1850 census, New York's House delegation shrank from 34 to 33 seats.

events.title: 1860 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1860 census, New York's House delegation shrank from 33 to 31 seats.

events.title: 1870 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1870 census, New York's House delegation grew from 31 to 33 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 43rd Congress (1873–1875), New York elected one of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1880 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1880 census, New York's House delegation grew from 33 to 34 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 48th Congress (1883–1885), New York elected one of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1890 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1890 census, New York kept 34 seats in the House.

events.title: 1900 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1900 census, New York's House delegation grew from 34 to 37 seats.

events.title: 1910 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1910 census, New York's House delegation grew from 37 to 43 seats.

events.title: 1930 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1930 census, New York's House delegation grew from 43 to 45 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 73rd through 78th Congresses (1933–1945), New York elected 2 of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1940 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1940 census, New York kept 45 seats in the House.

events.title: 1950 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1950 census, New York's House delegation shrank from 45 to 43 seats.

events.title: 1960 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1960 census, New York's House delegation shrank from 43 to 41 seats.

events.title: Wells v. Rockefeller
events.text: The Supreme Court struck down New York's congressional map because districts differed in population without adequate justification.

events.title: 1970 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1970 census, New York's House delegation shrank from 41 to 39 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1980 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1980 census, New York's House delegation shrank from 39 to 34 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1990 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1990 census, New York's House delegation shrank from 34 to 31 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 2000 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2000 census, New York's House delegation shrank from 31 to 29 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 2010 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2010 census, New York's House delegation shrank from 29 to 27 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 2020 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2020 census, New York's House delegation shrank from 27 to 26 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Harkenrider v. Hochul
events.text: New York's highest court ruled in April 2022 that the legislature's map was enacted through an improper process and drawn with partisan intent barred by the state constitution. A map drawn by a court-appointed special master was used in 2022.

events.title: Hoffmann v. Independent Redistricting Commission
events.text: In December 2023 the Court of Appeals ordered the Independent Redistricting Commission to resume work on a congressional map. The legislature adopted a new map in February 2024, used from the 2024 election.

events.title: NY-11 ruling stayed
events.text: A state trial court ordered the 11th District redrawn in January 2026, finding it diluted Black and Latino votes. The U.S. Supreme Court stayed that order in March 2026, and the 2024 map was used in the 2026 election.

compactnessNote: Polsby-Popper compactness (4π × area ÷ perimeter²) measured on the projected district shapes. It describes shape only: coastlines, rivers and county lines lower it too, so a low score is not evidence of intent. "Irregular" marks the least compact 5% of district shapes in each census era nationally.

c003.text: New map drawn after the 1790 census, which raised New York's seats from 6 to 10. It was first used in the 1792 election.

c006.text: In March 1797 the legislature redrew New York's ten congressional districts to reflect newly created counties. They are the first New York districts known by number.

c008.text: New map drawn after the 1800 census, which raised New York's seats from 10 to 17. It was first used in the 1802 election.

c009.text: A March 1804 state law combined the two New York City-area districts into one district that elected two members on a single ticket.

c011.text: On April 8, 1808, the legislature redrew New York's districts again, separating the combined New York City-area district. Two districts, the 2nd (including New York City) and the 6th (upstate), each elected two members.

c013.text: New map drawn after the 1810 census, which raised New York's seats from 17 to 27. It was first used in the 1812 election.

c017.text: Not a new map: the historical boundary records show only slight differences in 2 districts from the previous Congress, and no statewide redistricting is recorded for this election.

c018.text: New map drawn after the 1820 census, which raised New York's seats from 27 to 34. It was first used in the 1822 election.

c023.text: New map drawn after the 1830 census, which raised New York's seats from 34 to 40. It was first used in the 1832 election.

c028.text: New map drawn after the 1840 census, which cut New York's seats from 40 to 34. It was first used in the 1842 election.

c033.text: New map drawn after the 1850 census, which cut New York's seats from 34 to 33. It was first used in the 1852 election.

c034.text: Not a new map: the historical boundary records show only slight differences in 2 districts from the previous Congress, and no statewide redistricting is recorded for this election.

c038.text: New map drawn after the 1860 census, which cut New York's seats from 33 to 31. It was first used in the 1862 election.

c043.text: New map drawn after the 1870 census, which raised New York's seats from 31 to 33. It was first used in the 1872 election.

c044.text: In 1872 New York elected 32 members from districts and one statewide, for a seat Congress added in a supplemental apportionment that May. Before the 1874 election the legislature redrew the map into 33 districts.

c048.text: New map drawn after the 1880 census, which raised New York's seats from 33 to 34. It was first used in the 1882 election.

c049.text: The legislature had not redrawn the map in time for 1882 after New York gained a seat, so one seat was elected statewide. Before the 1884 election it redrew the districts to cover every seat.

c053.text: New map drawn after the 1890 census, which left New York with 34 seats. It was first used in the 1892 election.

c058.text: New map drawn after the 1900 census, which raised New York's seats from 34 to 37. It was first used in the 1902 election.

c063.text: New map drawn after the 1910 census, which raised New York's seats from 37 to 43. It was first used in the 1912 election.

c065.text: Not a new map: the historical boundary records show only slight differences in 2 districts from the previous Congress, and no statewide redistricting is recorded for this election.

c066.text: A 1917 state law (Laws of 1917, ch. 797) redrew the 3rd through 10th Districts. New York's highest court upheld the law in 1918.

c068.text: Not a new map: the historical boundary records show only slight differences in 3 districts from the previous Congress, and no statewide redistricting is recorded for this election.

c073.text: After the 1930 census raised New York's seats from 43 to 45, the state kept its existing districts and elected 2 members statewide (at-large).

c079.text: New map drawn after the 1940 census, which left New York with 45 seats. It was first used in the 1944 election.

c083.text: New map drawn after the 1950 census, which cut New York's seats from 45 to 43. It was first used in the 1952 election.

c088.text: New map drawn after the 1960 census, which cut New York's seats from 43 to 41. It was first used in the 1962 election.

c091.text: After a 1967 federal court ruling in Wells v. Rockefeller found New York's districts unequal in population, the legislature enacted a new congressional map in February 1968 for that year's election.

c092.text: After the Supreme Court in Wells v. Rockefeller (1969) barred use of the 1968 map in the 1970 election, the legislature passed a new congressional map in January 1970.

c093.text: New map drawn after the 1970 census, which cut New York's seats from 41 to 39. It was first used in the 1972 election.

c094.text: In 1974 the U.S. Justice Department objected under the Voting Rights Act to some 1972 district lines in Kings County (Brooklyn). The state then redrew those lines, including congressional districts.

c098.text: New map drawn after the 1980 census, which cut New York's seats from 39 to 34. It was first used in the 1982 election.

c099.text: New York's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1984 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c103.text: New map drawn after the 1990 census, which cut New York's seats from 34 to 31. It was first used in the 1992 election.

c106.text: In Diaz v. Silver (1997) a federal court ruled that race and ethnicity were the main factors in drawing the 12th District, making it unconstitutional. The legislature redrew the district and nearby lines in 1997.

c108.text: New map drawn after the 2000 census, which cut New York's seats from 31 to 29. It was first used in the 2002 election.

c113.text: New map drawn after the 2010 census, which cut New York's seats from 29 to 27. It was first used in the 2012 election.

c115.text: New York's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 2016 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c118.text: New map following: Harkenrider v. Hochul. New York's highest court ruled in April 2022 that the legislature's map was enacted through an improper process and drawn with partisan intent barred by the state constitution. A map drawn by a court-appointed special master was used in 2022.

c119.text: New map following: Hoffmann v. Independent Redistricting Commission. In December 2023 the Court of Appeals ordered the Independent Redistricting Commission to resume work on a congressional map. The legislature adopted a new map in February 2024, used from the 2024 election.
